newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Italy looks rosier, but snags ahead.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Italy looks rosier, but snags ahead.

text.p: Italy, desperate to catch the single European currency boat at its launch, received a series of promising signs this week, analysts said on Friday.
But bond convergence plays for BTPs, while offering some potential, still face snags, they said.
"Italy's chances of getting in have never been so high," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.

On Thursday Bundesbank's President Hans Tietmeyer -- a staunch defender of rigid interpretation of criteria for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- said Italy had the same chance as every other country to join.
Italy received a further boost on Friday amid expectations France and Germany were set to agree on a compromise for an EMU stability pact emphasising employment.
While officially there has been no news of a Franco-German accord, there has been speculation the three percent deficit-to-GDP target might not be applied strictly.

What's more, the OECD has come out with a peripheral-friendly forecast, saying Italy was neck-and-neck with France and Germany in the race to cut budget deficits to the three percent level. It saw all three at 3.2 percent by the EMU entry deadline.
"If the French don't make any further effort to correct the 1997 budget then there is a chance that Italy comes out in line with France even if it misses the three percent target," Giordano said.
But despite perceptions of Bonn taking a more lax tone towards Italy, analysts said the domestic scene was dogged by economic woes that could hamper Rome's ability to join EMU.
Bond analysts said convergence would soon hit a brick wall, especially in the short end of the Italian curve.
Ricardo Antoniol, economist for BankAmerica in Milan, said the 10-year BTP/Bund yield spread could narrow to around 110 basis points in a relatively short period of time from around 140 now.
But he would avoid the short end, which was prone to a tightening of monetary policy if inflation raised its head again in the summer.
Other analysts said investors should not to be whipsawed by the surge in optimism towards Italy.
Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London, expected the BTP/Bund spread to reach 200 basis points in the third quarter after an easing by 10-20 basis points in the short term.
"I'd better not tell you our forecast for the fourth quarter," Morris said, pegging this at 300 basis points.
"It's a non-consensus view and predicated on the idea that at the end of the day we are going to get a tumultuous end to EMU," said Morris.
He said a deal to mollify the stability pact could hit a constitutional snag in Germany which it ratified on condition that the criteria would be strictly adhered to.
Others said Italy's budget deficit was unlikely to squeeze into the three percent criteria.

"The Italian economy is still suffering and it will put pressure on the Bank of Italy to cut rates," said Morris, adding that could prompt a speculative attack on the lira and hit other peripheral bonds.
Another sore point is pension reform.
Giordano said a surge in early retirement before the government's plans for further pension reforms could hurt Italian bonds.
Analysts said other peripherals like Spain and Portugal had rosier prospects, although Spain's further convergence towards Bunds was seen as limited.
Spanish inflation moderated to 1.5 percent in May, but analysts said the Bank of Spain would hold off before sanctioning another rate cut.
"A cut is unlikely next Monday, but quite likely this month," Cesar Molinas, chief economist for FG Inversiones in Madrid told Reuters Financial Television.
Giordano of CSFB said, "In Spain I like the short end, probably the three year sector," adding that the Spanish curve would steepen.
